paragraph: How a person goes down is named. Jacob would go "mourning" and "with sorrow". David asks Solomon not to let Joab's gray head "go down to Sheol in peace", and to bring Shimei's down "with blood" (1 Kings 2:6, 9). A psalmist asks that the wicked "go silently to Sheol" (Psalm 31:17). Korah's company "went down alive into Sheol" (Numbers 16:33). The betrayed psalmist asks the same for those who had been his companions, "for evil is in their dwelling place and in their heart" (Psalm 55:13–15).

paragraph: **Wanting to go back.** "But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how can you turn back again to the weak and worthless elementary principles of the world, whose slaves you want to be once more?" (Galatians 4:9). "Tell me, you who desire to be under the law, do you not listen to the law?" (4:21). Paul is "afraid I may have labored over you in vain" (4:11). After the defeat at Ai, when "the hearts of the people melted", Joshua said, "Would that we had been content to dwell beyond the Jordan!" (Joshua 7:5, 7). In a figure: "no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says, 'The old is good'" (Luke 5:39). I read the will turning back toward what it knew, even toward slavery, when the new has cost something.

The verses ask in whose eyes, and by whose delight, a choice is good. They give more than one answer, and the setting decides which.
- **The chooser's own eyes.** *"if it is evil in your eyes to serve the Lord, choose this day"* (Joshua 24:15). Joshua leaves the view to the people, and the turning away from the Lord could begin there.
- **The Lord's eyes.** *"you did what was evil in my eyes"* (Isaiah 65:12).
- **The Lord's delight, not met.** *"chose what I did not delight in"* (65:12); *"chose that in which I did not delight"* (66:4).
- **The Lord's delight, met.** *"who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant"* (Isaiah 56:4). "Please" is the same word as "delight" in 65:12 and 66:4.
- **The soul's own delight, set against his.** *"their soul delights in their abominations"* (66:3), again the same word.
- **Other people's eyes, set against his choosing.** When God chooses, the verses often name a second measure held by the people around: *"everyone doing whatever is right in his own eyes"*, set against *"the place that the Lord your God will choose"* (Deuteronomy 12:8, 11); Michal's *"before the eyes of his servants' female servants"* against David's *"before the Lord"* (2 Samuel 6:20–21); a people despised *"in their sight"* (Jeremiah 33:24); *"rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen"* (1 Peter 2:4). See *Others around a choice*, below.
- **One's own "better", set against his word.** *"But Naaman was angry and went away, saying, 'Behold, I thought that he would surely come out to me …' Are not Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel?"* (2 Kings 5:11–12). His own measure ("better") and his own picture of how it should go ("I thought") stood against the prophet's word. His servants answered with a question: *"My father, it is a great word the prophet has spoken to you; will you not do it? Has he actually said to you, 'Wash, and be clean'?"* (5:13). He went down, and *"his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child"* (5:14). A measure of "better" nearly cost him the cure, and a question let him lay it down.
- **The king's eyes, or God's.** Saul proposed to pursue by night, "And they said, 'Do whatever seems good to you.' But the priest said, 'Let us draw near to God here'" (1 Samuel 14:36). God did not answer that day (14:37). When Saul swore that the guilty would die "though it be in Jonathan my son", "there was not a man among all the people who answered him", and then again, "Do what seems good to you" (14:39–40). The people give the king's eyes as the measure. The priest asks for God's first.
- **Another's will, given the whole decision.** Haman asks, "If it please the king, let it be decreed that they be destroyed" (Esther 3:9). The king gives him his ring and says, "The money is given to you, the people also, to do with them as it seems good to you" (3:11). Later the same king says to Esther and Mordecai, "you may write as you please with regard to the Jews … for an edict written in the name of the king and sealed with the king's ring cannot be revoked" (8:8). The measure is handed over twice, and the first handing cannot be undone.
- **The king's pleasure, asked for.** The same words come from the asking side. Nehemiah, asked what he was requesting, first "prayed to the God of heaven", then said, "If it pleases the king, and if your servant has found favor in your sight, that you send me to Judah" (Nehemiah 2:4–5). When it was granted he named another measure behind the king's: "And the king granted me what I asked, for the good hand of my God was upon me" (2:8). Memucan put his counsel against Vashti the same way, "If it please the king, let a royal order go out from him" (Esther 1:19), but what drove it was the fear that the women would "look at their husbands with contempt" (1:17). Esther kept the form after the king had offered "even to the half of my kingdom" (5:3): "If it please the king, let the king and Haman come today to a feast that I have prepared for the king" (5:4), and again when he asked her a second time (9:12–13). I read the form as leaving the decision with the king each time, even when he had offered to hand it over. What stands behind the asking differs: prayer, the fear of contempt, silver (Haman, above), a life (7:3).

**The one plotted against.** The verses also give the inner life of the person a plot is aimed at.
- **He may not know.** *"But I was like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter. I did not know it was against me they devised schemes"* (Jeremiah 11:19). He hands the matter to the one who sees inside: *"O Lord of hosts, who judges righteously, who tests the heart and the mind … to you have I committed my cause"* (11:20).
- **He prays to be guarded, and that the plan will not go forward.** *"Guard me, O Lord, from the hands of the wicked; preserve me from violent men, who have planned to trip up my feet"* (Psalm 140:4). *"Grant not, O Lord, the desires of the wicked; do not further their evil plot"* (140:8). *"Let them be turned back and disappointed who devise evil against me!"* (Psalm 35:4).
- **He trusts while it goes on.** After the whispering and the scheming, *"But I trust in you, O Lord; I say, 'You are my God.' My times are in your hand"* (Psalm 31:14–15). The plotters plan his time, and he puts his times in God's hand.
- **Someone else may plead.** Esther *"fell at his feet and wept and pleaded with him to avert the evil plan of Haman the Agagite and the plot that he had devised against the Jews"* (Esther 8:3). Haman had *"plotted against the Jews to destroy them, and had cast Pur"* (9:24).
- **Someone else may stop it.** In the shipwreck, *"The soldiers' plan was to kill the prisoners, lest any should swim away and escape. But the centurion, wishing to save Paul, kept them from carrying out their plan"* (Acts 27:42–43). One man's wish for one prisoner stopped a plan against all of them.

The verses describe God's anger in pictures, and they keep the pictures.
- **Fire, smoke and breath:** "By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of his anger they are consumed" (Job 4:9). "Why does your anger smoke against the sheep of your pasture?" (Psalm 74:1).
- **A poured liquid:** "he has poured out his fury like fire" (Lamentations 2:4).
- **A cup.** "Take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath, and make all the nations to whom I send you drink it" (Jeremiah 25:15). It is drunk to the dregs and then taken away: "Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of staggering … and I will put it into the hand of your tormentors" (Isaiah 51:22–23). A man's wrath is also poured as a drink: "Woe to him who makes his neighbors drink—you pour out your wrath and make them drunk" (Habakkuk 2:15), and "The cup in the Lord's right hand will come around to you" (2:16).
- **A storm:** "Behold, the storm of the Lord! Wrath has gone forth, a whirling tempest; it will burst upon the head of the wicked" (Jeremiah 23:19).
- **Weight:** "Your wrath lies heavy upon me" (Psalm 88:7).
- **In the New Testament,** it is revealed (Romans 1:18), stored up (Romans 2:5), it remains (John 3:36), and it is finished (Revelation 15:1).

The breath that gives life is also named in his anger. "By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of his anger they are consumed" (Job 4:9). "I will gather you and blow on you with the fire of my wrath" (Ezekiel 22:21). Chapter 2 follows the breath that gives life.

Job pictures friends who fail as a dry stream: *"My brothers are treacherous as a torrent-bed, as torrential streams that pass away, which are dark with ice, and where the snow hides itself. When they melt, they disappear; when it is hot, they vanish from their place"* (Job 6:15–17). Caravans turn aside to them and perish (6:18). A wadi runs full in the cold, when no one needs it, and is dry in the heat, when the travellers come. I read friends who are there when they are not needed and gone when they are.

Care for another's body is something Job swears to before God: *"if I have seen anyone perish for lack of clothing, or the needy without covering, if his body has not blessed me, and if he was not warmed with the fleece of my sheep"* (Job 31:19–20). The body that was warmed is pictured as blessing the one who warmed it.

The same verse that warns the kings opens a way out: "Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and you perish in the way, for his wrath is quickly kindled. Blessed are all who take refuge in him" (Psalm 2:12).

section: Soul, spirit and heart at death
paragraph: And one thing I did not expect: **the heart can die before the body does**. When Nabal sobered up and heard how close he had come to disaster, "his heart died within him, and he became as a stone. And about ten days later the Lord struck Nabal, and he died" (1 Samuel 25:37–38). The heart died first; the man died ten days later. The psalmist knows a similar death in life: "I have been forgotten like one who is dead; I have become like a broken vessel" (Psalm 31:12). Literally, forgotten *from the heart*.

paragraph: Splendour also passes. *"But the wicked will perish; the enemies of the Lord are like the glory of the pastures; they vanish—like smoke they vanish away"* (Psalm 37:20). The psalm opens, *"Fret not yourself because of evildoers; be not envious of wrongdoers!"* (37:1; *Jealousy and envy*). I read the figure as an answer to the envy: what might be envied is the bloom of a field, and smoke.

section: Soul, spirit and heart at death
paragraph:
**The soul.**
- **It departs.** "As her soul was departing (for she was dying), she called his name Ben-oni" (Genesis 35:18).
- **It dies.** Balaam: "Let me die the death of the upright, and let my end be like his!" (Numbers 23:10). Samson: "Let me die with the Philistines" (Judges 16:30). In both, the Hebrew is *let my soul die*. And "the soul who sins shall die" (Ezekiel 18:4).
- **It is poured out.** Of the servant: "he poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors" (Isaiah 53:12). Before his death Jesus said, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death" (Matthew 26:38).
- **It is named to the very end.** Even the corpse is *nephesh* ("soul"): "Whoever touches the dead body of any person" (Numbers 19:11).
- **It has an end beyond death, and Psalm 49 names two.** The psalm is about the death that comes to everyone: "even the wise die; the fool and the stupid alike must perish" (Psalm 49:10). Of the man who trusts in his wealth: "his soul will go to the generation of his fathers, who will never again see light" (49:19). Of himself, the psalmist says: "But God will ransom my soul from the power of Sheol, for he will receive me" (49:15). The psalm does not say what being received involves, and I do not fill it in. Of those who trust in their wealth it says, "death shall be their shepherd, and the upright shall rule over them in the morning" (49:14), and it draws a word for the living from this: "Be not afraid when a man becomes rich" (49:16).
- **It is not abandoned.** David wrote, "you will not abandon my soul to Sheol, or let your holy one see corruption" (Psalm 16:10). Peter reads it of Christ's death and rising: "he was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption" (Acts 2:31).

The proverbs judge a desire by where it ends: *"The desire of the righteous ends only in good, the expectation of the wicked in wrath"* (Proverbs 11:23). The psalm sets the end beside a sight. The righteous man *"has distributed freely; he has given to the poor … his horn is exalted in honor. The wicked man sees it and is angry; he gnashes his teeth and melts away; the desire of the wicked will perish!"* (Psalm 112:9–10). No word for envy is used there. The verse names the sight, the anger and the end of the desire.

section: On God's word, and on God
paragraph:
Delight in God's word is said beside other inner acts, and it does not take their place.
- **Beside fear.** "Blessed is the man who fears the Lord, who greatly delights in his commandments!" (Psalm 112:1). Fear and delight are said of one man in one breath (*Fear* above).
- **Beside asking to be led.** "Lead me in the path of your commandments, for I delight in it. Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to selfish gain!" (Psalm 119:35–36). He gives his delight as the reason to be led, and in the next breath asks for his heart to be inclined. I read that delighting in the way does not make a man able to steer himself on it.
- **Beside not forgetting, and love.** "I will delight in your statutes; I will not forget your word" (Psalm 119:16), "as much as in all riches" (119:14). "I find my delight in your commandments, which I love" (119:47).
- **Beside meditating.** "but his delight is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he meditates day and night" (Psalm 1:2). The "but" sets the delight against the counsel, the way and the seat of the wicked (1:1). What he delights in he turns over day and night (10.4). I read the psalm naming the man by what he delights in, more than by what he avoids.
- **Under pressure.** The delight is held where other things press on it. While "princes sit plotting against me" (Psalm 119:23): "Your testimonies are my delight; they are my counselors" (119:24). What he delights in also counsels him. In affliction: "If your law had not been my delight, I would have perished in my affliction" (119:92). He does not say the law kept him, but his delight in it, and goes on, "I will never forget your precepts, for by them you have given me life" (119:93; 10.3). In anguish: "Trouble and anguish have found me out, but your commandments are my delight" (119:143). The trouble is not taken away. The delight stands beside it.
- **Joined to doing.** "I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart" (Psalm 40:8). The delight is in doing, and the law is inward. Two verses before, it is God who has "not delighted" in sacrifice (40:6; 13.1).
- **Inward, and at war.** "For I delight in the law of God, in my inner being, but I see in my members another law waging war against the law of my mind" (Romans 7:22–23). The delight is real and it is inward, and it does not carry the members with it. The cry that follows is in Chapter 2 (7:24), and the divided service in Chapter 7 (7:25).

The one it is set for prays out of his weakness. "When my spirit faints within me, you know my way! In the path where I walk they have hidden a trap for me" (Psalm 142:3). "No one cares for my soul" (142:4). It is worse when it comes from those he had prayed for: "Yet they have dug a pit for my life. Remember how I stood before you to speak good for them" (Jeremiah 18:20).

section: Breath lent, and held by God
paragraph:
Life is held in the breath, and the breath is God's to give and to take back.
- "In his hand is the life of every living thing and the breath of all mankind" (Job 12:10).
- Daniel tells a king who had praised idols that he had not honoured "the God in whose hand is your breath, and whose are all your ways" (Daniel 5:23).
- "If he should set his heart to it and gather to himself his spirit and his breath, all flesh would perish together, and man would return to dust" (Job 34:14–15).
- "When you take away their breath, they die and return to their dust. When you send forth your Spirit, they are created" (Psalm 104:29–30).
- "No man has power to retain the spirit, or power over the day of death" (Ecclesiastes 8:8).
- "When his breath departs, he returns to the earth; on that very day his plans perish" (Psalm 146:4). Thinking goes when the breath goes. "Man is like a breath; his days are like a passing shadow" (Psalm 144:4), and the Lord "knows the thoughts of man, that they are but a breath" (Psalm 94:11).

The same death is met in different ways. "One dies in his full vigor, being wholly at ease and secure"; "Another dies in bitterness of soul, never having tasted of prosperity" (Job 21:23, 25). Nothing goes with the dead: "For when he dies he will carry nothing away; his glory will not go down after him" (Psalm 49:17); "When the wicked dies, his hope will perish" (Proverbs 11:7). No one knows when it will come: "I am old; I do not know the day of my death" (Genesis 27:2). Yet the Preacher can write that "the day of death" is better "than the day of birth" (Ecclesiastes 7:1).

section: Care, discouragement and hiding between people
paragraph:
What one person carries inside can be for another, or done to another.
- **Care for another is a good anxiety.** Paul's "daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches" is to be weak with the weak (2 Corinthians 11:28–29). Members of one body are to "have the same care for one another" (1 Corinthians 12:25). Section 10.1 sets out the difference between this care and anxiety for oneself.
- **Losing heart is done by another.** "Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged" (Colossians 3:21). Every use of the words for losing heart has another party behind it (10.1).
- **A whisperer separates friends.** "A whisperer separates close friends" (Proverbs 16:28), and "where there is no whisperer, quarreling ceases" (26:20) (10.5).
- **People hide from people, and hide one another.** The weaker side hides: "When the wicked rise, people hide themselves" (Proverbs 28:28). Rahab and Obadiah hid others to keep them alive (Joshua 2:4; 1 Kings 18:4). And no one can hide from a friend who turns: "it is not an adversary who deals insolently with me — then I could hide from him. But it is you, a man, my equal" (Psalm 55:12–13). Section 10.11 follows all of this.

Much of the hiding in Scripture is from people who could do harm, and in these verses it is the weaker side that hides. "When the wicked rise, people hide themselves" (Proverbs 28:28). "The poor of the earth all hide themselves" (Job 24:4). When Israel hid in the caves, "all the people followed him trembling" (1 Samuel 13:7).

The Preacher sets another sight beside this. "There is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness, and there is a wicked man who prolongs his life in his evildoing" (Ecclesiastes 7:15). And he adds: "Though a sinner does evil a hundred times and prolongs his life, yet I know that it will be well with those who fear God" (8:12). Scripture states both. I leave them side by side.

- **Which way it faces.** For someone or against them. "Discretion will watch over you" (Proverbs 2:11). "All their thoughts are against me for evil" (Psalm 56:5). But "against" alone does not decide it. God's plan against a nation is open to its turning: "if that nation … turns from its evil, I will relent" (Jeremiah 18:8). What decides is what the act is *for*.
- **The company it keeps.** Discretion keeps company with knowledge and prudence (Proverbs 1:4; 8:12), the evil device with arrogance and pride (Psalm 10:2, 4) and a quick temper (Proverbs 14:17). Plans are established by counsel (Proverbs 20:18) and by being committed to the Lord (16:3). Whispering together makes a plot (Psalm 41:7).
- **The state of the heart it rises from.** The same tender heart is cowardice in one place and repentance in another (Deuteronomy 20:8; 2 Kings 22:19, above). Paul names the order of cause: people are "darkened in their understanding … due to their hardness of heart" (Ephesians 4:18).
- **Ease or distress.** "In the thought of one who is at ease there is contempt for misfortune" (Job 12:5). Under suffering, God's reckoning is felt as enmity: "Why do you hide your face and count me as your enemy?" (Job 13:24). This is still a small set of verses, and I hold it loosely.
- **Distress turns people both ways.** In distress Manasseh "humbled himself greatly" (2 Chronicles 33:12), and Ahaz "became yet more faithless" (28:22). The texts set the cases side by side without saying why. Ease cuts both ways too: "I am exceedingly angry with the nations that are at ease" (Zechariah 1:15).
- **What it is joined with.** Anger joined with grief heals (Mark 3:5). Joined with jealousy, it "will accept no compensation" (Proverbs 6:34–35).
- **How long it lasts.** For anger, time is part of what it is. It is to end before sunset (Ephesians 4:26). It turns away as a brother forgets (Genesis 27:45). God's is "but for a moment" (Psalm 30:5). Edom "kept his wrath forever" (Amos 1:11).
- **Whether it is seen truly.** Anger kindled by a lie still acts (Genesis 39:19). The heavy hand of God, felt from fear, is misread (Matthew 25:24–25).
- **The answer it meets.** "A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger" (Proverbs 15:1). A question, or a new way of seeing, does more than a rebuke (Genesis 4:6; 45:8; Luke 15:32).
- **What the one who brings it brings first.** The same offering is refused and then delighted in, and what comes between is a broken heart (Psalm 51:16–19, §4 above). The same weakness is pleaded against and then pleases, and what comes between is God's answer (2 Corinthians 12:8–10).
- **Haste or a pause.** "Everyone who is hasty comes only to poverty" (Proverbs 21:5). "Be not quick in your spirit to become angry" (Ecclesiastes 7:9). "The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer" (Proverbs 15:28).
- **Where it happens.** The bed holds plotting and prayer (Psalm 36:4; 63:6). But one place does change what thinking can see: "until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end" (Psalm 73:17).
- **What it is turned toward.** At the sea "they feared greatly" as Egypt marched (Exodus 14:10). After the crossing, "the people feared the Lord, and they believed in the Lord" (14:31). The sailors "were afraid" in the storm, and when the sea was calm "the men feared the Lord exceedingly" (Jonah 1:5, 16). Fear of man is set against him: "who are you that you are afraid of man who dies … and have forgotten the Lord, your Maker" (Isaiah 51:12–13). The same holds for refusing and choosing. Refusing the evil is right and refusing the gentle waters is wrong (Isaiah 7:15; 8:6). The act is the same, and what it is aimed at decides. The one knowing is turned to right and wrong, to taste and to judgement (Isaiah 7:15; 2 Samuel 19:35; Job 34:4). The one verb for choosing is turned to whatever is set before a person (10.7). The soul's desire is allowed for meat in the towns and for the Levite's coming to the chosen place (Deuteronomy 12:21; 18:6), and the soul's delight in abominations goes with a wrong choice (Isaiah 66:3).
- **Whether the heart is in it.** Fear of God can be "a commandment taught by men" while "their hearts are far from me" (Isaiah 29:13). God promises the other: "I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me" (Jeremiah 32:40).
- **Who chooses.** When God chooses a person, the inner life is what the choosing is for: "that you may know and believe me and understand" (Isaiah 43:10). When people choose a person, the inner life is what they choose by (Acts 6:3, 5). The same verb is used of both (10.7).
- **Whose eyes, and whose delight.** "Evil in your eyes" is where turning from the Lord could begin (Joshua 24:15), and "good to you" is a choice the king honours (2 Samuel 19:38). In Joshua the choice is between the Lord and other gods. With Barzillai it is where an old man who served will live. Delight is the soul's own in Isaiah 66:3 and the Lord's in 65:12 and 56:4. The word is the same; whose it is decides (10.7). When God chooses, the people around often hold another measure: "everyone doing whatever is right in his own eyes" (Deuteronomy 12:8), "before the eyes of his servants' female servants" (2 Samuel 6:20), "in their sight" (Jeremiah 33:24), "rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen" (1 Peter 2:4). The words "what seems good to you" carry different acts: loyalty in Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 19:27), fear in the rulers before Jehu (2 Kings 10:5), a cover in the men of Jabesh (1 Samuel 11:10), a people handed over in a king's word (Esther 3:11), and yielding to God in Eli and David (1 Samuel 3:18; 2 Samuel 15:26). The words are the same; the setting decides (10.7, 10.10, 10.11).
- **Who speaks it, and to what end.** The same words of comfort, "do not fear", come from God, from a friend, and from one who means harm (§4 above; 10.5; 10.10).
- **Whose mouth it is in.** That God delights in a man is thanks from the one rescued and a taunt from those who watch him suffer (Psalm 18:19; 22:8, §4 above).
- **Who hears it.** The same scroll was read to the officials and to the king. The officials "turned one to another in fear" (Jeremiah 36:16). The king and his servants "who heard all these words" were not afraid (36:24).
- **Whether it pulls the person to many things or to one.** Martha was "anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary" (Luke 10:41–42). Paul wants "undivided devotion to the Lord" (1 Corinthians 7:35). The double-minded man is "unstable in all his ways" (James 1:8).
- **Who acts on whom.** God hiding a person is safety, and God hiding his face is dismay (Psalm 27:5, 9). Losing heart is always done by another (10.1).
- **Whether it is brought before God.** "When I am afraid, I put my trust in you" (Psalm 56:3). Many cares, met by his consolations (Psalm 94:19). Anxiety made known to God, and his peace guarding the heart (Philippians 4:6–7). Thoughts offered to be searched (Psalm 139:23). Thoughts taken "captive to obey Christ" (2 Corinthians 10:5).
- **What comes back.** What is devised returns on the deviser (Esther 9:25; Micah 2:1–3), and the diligent plan returns as abundance (Proverbs 21:5).
- **What it is set against.** "To live" is said of a span of years, of escaping hunger or the sword, of recovering from illness, of the dead given life again, and of the heart and spirit revived (Chapter 2). The verses pair it with what it escapes: "that we may live and not die" (Genesis 42:2); "so turn, and live" (Ezekiel 18:32); "why will you die, O house of Israel?" (33:11). The breath God gives can come back out of a person as lies: "a false witness breathes out lies" (Proverbs 14:5).
- **What brings it about, and who acts.** "Die" is said of the body's end, of a sentence passed by people, of a judgment from God, of the end of a way taken, and of something that happens inside a living person: "sin came alive and I died" (Romans 7:9); "Whoever does not love abides in death" (1 John 3:14). It is said of a death undergone on purpose: "How can we who died to sin still live in it?" (Romans 6:2). It is said of a death that belongs to the Lord: "if we die, we die to the Lord" (Romans 14:8). The verses name what brings death: sin (Romans 5:12), "vexation" and "jealousy" (Job 5:2), "the desire of the sluggard" (Proverbs 21:25), and God, who says "I kill and I make alive" (Deuteronomy 32:39). "Put to death" is said both of executing a person and of "what is earthly in you" (Colossians 3:5). "Dead dog" is said of oneself in lowliness (2 Samuel 9:8) and of another in contempt (2 Samuel 16:9). Chapter 2 gives the account.
- **Who swears it, and what for.** "As the Lord lives" is said in loyalty (2 Kings 2:2), in anger (2 Samuel 12:5), in a rash vow the people overturn (1 Samuel 14:39, 45), and on the way to greed (2 Kings 5:20). The words stay the same. The verses give the measure: "in truth, in justice, and in righteousness" (Jeremiah 4:2).
- **What it is joined to.** "Long" is days promised with honouring parents (Exodus 20:12), the wicked who "prolongs his life in his evildoing" (Ecclesiastes 7:15), and, with anger, patience: "Good sense makes one slow to anger" (Proverbs 19:11). "Life" is something loathed (Job 10:1), and in Elihu's words it is itself what loathes: "his life loathes bread" (Job 33:20).
- **Who rouses, and toward what.** The same word for rousing is used when God rouses himself (Zechariah 2:13) and when he is begged to (Psalm 44:23). It is used when God stirs a spirit to build (Ezra 1:5) or to destroy (Jeremiah 51:1, 11), and when hatred stirs up strife (Proverbs 10:12). Love is not to be stirred "until it pleases" (Song of Songs 2:7). Its power shows when it is withheld: God "did not stir up all his wrath" (Psalm 78:38). And some things cannot be roused at all: the dead man "till the heavens are no more" (Job 14:12), and the idol with "no breath at all in it" (Habakkuk 2:19). Haggai gives the order on the building side: obedience, the fear of the Lord, "I am with you", then the stirring, then the work (Haggai 1:12–14; 13.1, *Stirring*).
- **Before whom it is said, and what it rests on.** "Eat, drink, be merry" is folly in the rich man who says it to his own soul over goods laid up (Luke 12:19–20), and it is commended by the Preacher as "his lot" in "the few days of his life that God has given him" (Ecclesiastes 5:18; 8:15). The words are nearly the same (10.6).
- **Whose jealousy, and for whom.** Jealousy is God's for his people against those who scorned them (Ezekiel 36:5), and over his people's own spirit, met with grace (James 4:5–6). It is Elijah's for God (1 Kings 19:10), Joshua's for Moses, refused by Moses (Numbers 11:29), a husband's that will take no compensation (Proverbs 6:34–35), and envy of the wicked that embitters the soul (Psalm 73:3, 21). The word stays the same. What differs is whose it is, whom it is for, and whether it wants God's gift kept narrow (10.6; 13.1). Zeal can be sincere, aimed at God and still wrong for lack of knowledge (Romans 10:2; Philippians 3:6). It consumes the one who has it (Psalm 69:9). It can be put on show (2 Kings 10:16), or set an oath aside (2 Samuel 21:2). Against a person it spoils what it cannot take (Genesis 26:14–15) and claims equality (Numbers 16:3; Psalm 106:16). A husband's jealousy, which may be wrong, is put before God (Numbers 5:14, 30).
- **What it is aimed at.** Job rouses himself against the godless and is upright in it (Job 17:8). He disowns rousing himself at an enemy's ruin (31:29). It is the same act of rousing oneself (10.10).
- **When the cost appears.** The nearer redeemer was willing for the land and unwilling when Ruth came with it (Ruth 4:4–6). The will turned when his own inheritance was touched (10.7).
- **Whose will, and whether it can carry itself out.** The same verb, "want", is a will that wants the good and cannot do it (Romans 7:19), a will asked out by Jesus, "What do you want me to do for you?" (Mark 10:51), a will made absolute (Daniel 11:3), a will that gives way to a crowd (Luke 23:25), and a will taken up and turned, "If anyone would be first" (Mark 9:35). Willing God's will comes before knowing it (John 7:17) (10.7).
- **Whom the need is spoken to.** The same thirst accuses Moses at Rephidim (Exodus 17:3) and asks God at Lehi (Judges 15:18) (10.6).

**Jealousy in the body and between people.** Envy reaches the bones: "A tranquil heart gives life to the flesh, but envy makes the bones rot" (Proverbs 14:30; Chapter 4). It can kill the one who has it: "jealousy slays the simple" (Job 5:2; 10.1). A husband's jealousy fixes the will: "He will accept no compensation" (Proverbs 6:34–35; 10.1, 10.7). And "who can stand before jealousy?" (Proverbs 27:4; 10.13). It ends with the life. Of the dead: *"Their love and their hate and their envy have already perished, and forever they have no more share in all that is done under the sun"* (Ecclesiastes 9:6; Chapter 2).

And the dead will wake. "Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt" (Daniel 12:2). The waking is not the same for all. Isaiah sets two kinds of dead side by side: "They are dead, they will not live; they are shades, they will not arise" (Isaiah 26:14), and "You who dwell in the dust, awake and sing for joy!" (26:19). For the psalmist, waking means seeing God: "when I awake, I shall be satisfied with your likeness" (Psalm 17:15). These verses are followed below, in "The body raised" and "Life, and judgment". Job's "he will not awake" stands beside them, and I do not reconcile the two.

paragraph:
The hope Scripture gives does not leave the body behind. Job says it of his own flesh: "For I know that my Redeemer lives, and at the last he will stand upon the earth. And after my skin has been thus destroyed, yet in my flesh I shall see God, whom I shall see for myself, and my eyes shall behold, and not another. My heart faints within me!" (Job 19:25–27). The psalmist says it of waking: "As for me, I shall behold your face in righteousness; when I awake, I shall be satisfied with your likeness" (Psalm 17:15).
- "Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise. You who dwell in the dust, awake and sing for joy! … the earth will give birth to the dead" (Isaiah 26:19).
- A few verses earlier, of other lords: "They are dead, they will not live; they are shades, they will not arise" (26:14).
- "After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him" (Hosea 6:2).

paragraph:
Some not-knowing is not the person's failure at all. The verses say the understanding was hidden from them. The words are those for hiding (*kruptō*, *parakaluptō*, "to hide, conceal"; *sātar*, "to hide").
- **Hidden for a time.** "They did not understand this saying, and it was concealed from them, so that they might not perceive it. And they were afraid to ask him about this saying" (Luke 9:45). The next verse: "An argument arose among them as to which of them was the greatest" (9:46). And again: "This saying was hidden from them, and they did not grasp what was said" (Luke 18:34).
- **Hidden as judgement.** Over Jerusalem: "Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes" (Luke 19:42). Isaiah: "the discernment of their discerning men shall be hidden" (Isaiah 29:14), of a people whose "hearts are far from me" (29:13).
- **Hidden by God, and given to others.** "I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children" (Matthew 11:25). Jesus says it in thanks.
- **Hidden from myself.** "Who can discern his errors? Declare me innocent from hidden faults" (Psalm 19:12). The psalm ends by handing the heart's meditation over to God's sight (19:14).

**Every activity can change character.** The same act of thinking is discretion in one person and an evil device in another. It is a plan against that is meant to bring people back, or a plot against the messenger (Jeremiah 18:11–18). What changes it is not the act itself. The verses point to its direction, the company it keeps, the state of the heart it rises from, its pace, and whether it is brought before God. Chapter 10.4 shows this for thinking, and Chapter 11 (§4) gathers it across all the activities.

**Hearing goes both ways.** The ear is the way in, and it is also where what goes out arrives. God hears what people say: "You have heard their taunts, O Lord, all their plots against me" (Lamentations 3:61). "Then those who feared the Lord spoke with one another. The Lord paid attention and heard them" (Malachi 3:16). And refusing to hear goes with devising. "I am bringing disaster upon this people, the fruit of their devices, because they have not paid attention to my words" (Jeremiah 6:19). Jeremiah's enemies plot against him with these words: "let us not pay attention to any of his words" (Jeremiah 18:18).

**One passage, three plans: Jeremiah 18.**
- God says, "Behold, I am shaping disaster against you and devising a plan against you. Return, every one from his evil way" (18:11). Even this plan is open: "if that nation … turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster that I intended to do to it" (18:8).
- The people answer, "We will follow our own plans, and will every one act according to the stubbornness of his evil heart" (18:12).
- Then they turn on the messenger: "Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah" (18:18).

section: The tongue, the lips and the eyes devise
paragraph:
Several verses give the tongue, the lips and the eyes the verbs of planning.
- "Your tongue plots destruction, like a sharp razor, you worker of deceit" (Psalm 52:2).
- "They do not speak peace, but against those who are quiet in the land they devise words of deceit" (Psalm 35:20).
- "Whoever winks his eyes plans dishonest things; he who purses his lips brings evil to pass" (Proverbs 16:30).
- "All who hate me whisper together about me; they imagine the worst for me" (Psalm 41:7).
- Jeremiah's enemies: "Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah … let us strike him with the tongue" (Jeremiah 18:18).

- **A tender heart.** It melts before an enemy and spreads fear to others (Deuteronomy 20:8). But Josiah's heart "was penitent [tender]" before God's word, and God answered him with peace (2 Kings 22:19–20). The same softness is cowardice in one place and repentance in the other.
- **A strong heart.** "Be strong, and let your heart take courage; wait for the Lord!" (Psalm 27:14). With Absalom, the same verb gives his servants the nerve to kill: "be courageous and be valiant" (2 Samuel 13:28). With Pharaoh it is hardening: "I will harden his heart" (Exodus 4:21), literally *strengthen*.
- **A guarded heart.** "Keep your heart with all vigilance" (Proverbs 4:23). Three chapters later the same word describes the adulteress, "wily [guarded] of heart" (Proverbs 7:10).
- **Crushing.** Crushed by an enemy, the spirit collapses (Psalm 143:3–4). Offered to God, a crushed spirit is the very sacrifice he wants: "a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" (Psalm 51:17).
- **Loving and hating one's own soul** (Chapter 5).
- **Devising.** The same Hebrew verb describes the craftsmen who worked cherubim "skillfully" into the tabernacle curtains (Exodus 26:1) and those who plot. One word for planning means "discretion" (Proverbs 2:11), "evil devices" (Proverbs 12:2), and God's own purpose: "no purpose of yours can be thwarted" (Job 42:2).
- **Planning against.** God says, "I am … devising a plan against you. Return" (Jeremiah 18:11), and the people say, "Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah" (18:18). The word and the "against" are the same. One plan is meant to bring people back, and the other is meant to silence the one who calls them.
- **Purposing.** The verb for purposing (*zāmam*) is the psalmist's resolve: "I have purposed that my mouth will not transgress" (Psalm 17:3). It is the wicked man's plot: "The wicked plots against the righteous" (Psalm 37:12). It is the wise woman's weighing: "She considers a field and buys it" (Proverbs 31:16). And it is God's fixed purpose: "I have purposed; I have not relented" (Jeremiah 4:28). I read the change as following whom it is aimed at: one's own mouth, another's harm, one's own household, or a whole land.
- **Willing.** The Hebrew word for being willing (*ʾāḇâ*) is almost always a "no". It is the guard's refusal to kill the priests (1 Samuel 22:17), David refusing the water for the men's sake (2 Samuel 23:17), Amnon refusing Tamar's plea (2 Samuel 13:14), and Israel refusing God's rest (Isaiah 30:15). God himself is "not willing to destroy" (2 Kings 8:19), and "will not be willing to forgive" the man who blesses himself in his stubbornness (Deuteronomy 29:20). The Greek word runs from Pilate "wishing to satisfy the crowd" (Mark 15:15) to God "not wishing that any should perish" (2 Peter 3:9). Each passage gives the reason: faith, honour, force, fear, grief, covenant, love, a self-blessing heart. I read the change as following what is refused, and for whose sake (10.7, *Willing*).
- **Planning ahead.** The same looking ahead is a king's honest count of his strength (Luke 14:31) and sailors' guess "on the chance that somehow" (Acts 27:12). It is a man's "aim in life" (2 Timothy 3:10) and a plot "to put him to death" (John 11:53). I read the verses as setting the difference beside how much the planner can see. The king can count, the sailors cannot see the reef, and over all of it "the Lord establishes his steps" (Proverbs 16:9).
- **Reckoning.** People misreckon: "we esteemed him stricken" (Isaiah 53:4). God reckons faith "as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6). The law reckons in order to release (Leviticus 25:50). Love refuses to reckon at all: it "is not … resentful" (1 Corinthians 13:5).
- **Likening.** Comparing is how love praises ("I compare you, my love", Song of Songs 1:9), how comfort reaches out (Lamentations 2:13), and how worship ends ("who in the skies can be compared to the Lord?", Psalm 89:6). It is also how pride rises: "I will make myself like the Most High" (Isaiah 14:14).
- **Reasoning.** The Greek word is Mary's honest pondering (Luke 1:29), the disciples' anxious circling (Mark 8:17), and a quarrel (Philippians 2:14; 1 Timothy 2:8).
- **The nose.** The Hebrew word for anger, *ʾaph*, is the nostril where God breathed in life (Genesis 2:7), the face bowed in worship (2 Chronicles 7:3), and the face lifted in pride (Psalm 10:4). It can be given a ring in love (Ezekiel 16:12) or a hook for raging (2 Kings 19:28). "Long of nostrils" is patience, in God and in the wise (Exodus 34:6; Proverbs 14:29).
- **Anger.** Jesus's anger heals (Mark 3:5). A crowd's anger stops its ears and kills (Acts 7:57–58). "Be angry and do not sin" (Ephesians 4:26).
- **Vexation.** It is provocation done to another (1 Samuel 1:6), suffering borne (1:16), and "Sorrow is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad" (Ecclesiastes 7:3).
- **Provoking.** Love "is not irritable" (1 Corinthians 13:5), with the same word that tells believers to "stir up one another to love and good works" (Hebrews 10:24).
- **Overflow.** One Hebrew word, *ʿebrah*, is the overflow of anger and the overflow of pride. God offers it to Job with irony: "Pour out the overflowings of your anger, and look on everyone who is proud and abase him" (Job 40:11). And "'Scoffer' is the name of the arrogant, haughty man who acts with arrogant pride" (Proverbs 21:24), where the word is the same.
- **Storm.** The same storm word, *sāʿar*, is the angry king's mind ("the mind of the king of Syria was greatly troubled", 2 Kings 6:11) and the suffering city ("O afflicted one, storm-tossed and not comforted", Isaiah 54:11).
- **Denouncing.** "How can I curse whom God has not cursed?" (Numbers 23:8). But "Whoever says to the wicked, 'You are in the right,' will be cursed by peoples, abhorred by nations" (Proverbs 24:24). The word is empty when it goes against God's verdict, and it lands when it follows justice.
- **A creed.** "Slow to anger" is used in worship, in pleading, in confession, in Jonah's complaint, in praise, in wonder, in announcing judgment, and as the ground for returning (Chapter 10.9).
- **Mourning.** Aaron is forbidden to mourn "lest … wrath come" (Leviticus 10:6). When the wrath has come, mourning is commanded (Jeremiah 4:8).
- **God's hand.** The "mighty hand" brought Israel out (Deuteronomy 6:21) and later fought "against you … in anger" (Jeremiah 21:5).
- **Fear.** One word, *yārēʾ*, "to fear", names the fear that drives a person away from God and the fear of God that keeps a person from sin. In one sentence Moses takes the first away and sets the second in its place: "Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you, that you may not sin" (Exodus 20:20). The same people, with the same word, are afraid of Egypt and then fear the Lord (Exodus 14:10, 31). Turned round, the word describes the one who is feared: "the great and awesome God, who keeps covenant and steadfast love" (Nehemiah 1:5). Beside a choice it has three more faces. It is learned at a feast in the place God chose: "that you may learn to fear the Lord your God always" (Deuteronomy 14:23). It falls on those who hear of presumption punished: "all the people shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again" (17:13). And it comes as terror on people who resisted God's choice once he made it plain: "Are we all to perish?" (Numbers 17:13). Section 10.1 sets out the word, and 10.7 the faces beside a choice.
- **"Do not fear."** God says it with a reason, and the reason is himself: "for I am with you" (Isaiah 41:10). Joseph says it and refuses to stand in God's place (Genesis 50:19, 21). Jael says it before the tent peg (Judges 4:18). The words are the same. What they are for is not.
- **Trembling and dread.** The Hebrew words for trembling and dread are rendered as fear, and also as "Be angry" (Psalm 4:4), "deeply moved" (2 Samuel 18:33), a heart that "trembled for the ark of God" (1 Samuel 4:13), and "your heart shall thrill and exult" (Isaiah 60:5). I read them as naming one inner stirring, which its situation turns into fear, anger, grief, care or joy (10.1).
- **"None shall make you afraid."** It is promised peace: "I will give peace in the land, and you shall lie down, and none shall make you afraid" (Leviticus 26:6). The same Hebrew phrase is used of desolation: "The cities of Aroer are deserted; they will be for flocks, which will lie down, and none will make them afraid" (Isaiah 17:2). One phrase describes rest for a people and the emptiness left when they are gone.
- **Care.** The Greek *merimnaō*, "to be anxious, to care", is rebuked when it is about my own food and clothing (Matthew 6:25) and praised when it is "genuinely concerned for your welfare" (Philippians 2:20). The Hebrew *dāʾag*, "to be anxious, to dread", is dread of what may come (Jeremiah 38:19), a father's worry for his son (1 Samuel 10:2), and sorrow for sin: "I am sorry for my sin" (Psalm 38:18). Section 10.1 sets this out.
- **Hiding.** The Hebrew *sātar*, "to hide", is God hiding a person in safety and God hiding his face, four verses apart (Psalm 27:5, 9), and a sinner asking God to hide his face from his sins (Psalm 51:9). A treasure is hidden "in his joy", and a talent hidden because "I was afraid" (Matthew 13:44; 25:25). Sections 10.9 and 10.11.
- **Murmuring.** The Hebrew *rāgan* is the people's complaint "in your tents" against God (Deuteronomy 1:27) and the whisperer's words that separate friends (Proverbs 16:28) (10.5).
- **Remembering.** It bows the soul down and it gives hope, in two consecutive verses (Lamentations 3:20–21; Chapter 10.3).
- **The bed.** It is the same place, but what happens there goes either way. "He plots trouble while on his bed" (Psalm 36:4). "I remember you upon my bed, and meditate on you in the watches of the night" (Psalm 63:6).
- **"Good" or "evil" in your eyes.** Joshua leaves the choice to the people's own sight: "if it is evil in your eyes to serve the Lord, choose this day" (Joshua 24:15). The king honours an old man's sight: "whatever seems good to you" (2 Samuel 19:38). In Isaiah the measure is the Lord's: "you did what was evil in my eyes" (Isaiah 65:12). Section 10.7 sets this out.
- **Knowing good and evil.** It is the child's knowing "how to refuse the evil and choose the good" (Isaiah 7:15). It is Barzillai's palate at eighty, with the same words: "Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not?" (2 Samuel 19:35). And it is the weighing of words in a dispute: "Let us choose what is right; let us know among ourselves what is good" (Job 34:4).
- **Refusing.** The Hebrew *māʾas*, "to refuse, reject, despise", is refusing the evil (Isaiah 7:15) and refusing "the waters of Shiloah that flow gently" (8:6). Elihu uses it of refusing God's terms (Job 34:33). Job turns it on himself: "therefore I despise myself, and repent" (42:6).
- **Choosing.** The Hebrew *bāḥar*, "to choose", is the choice of a master (Joshua 24:15), of a place to live (Deuteronomy 23:16), of a way (Psalm 119:30; Isaiah 66:3), of wisdom over silver (Proverbs 16:16), and of a verdict (Job 34:4).
- **Delight.** The Hebrew *ḥāpēṣ*, "to delight in", is the soul's own delight in what it chose: "their soul delights in their abominations" (Isaiah 66:3). It is also the Lord's delight as the measure of a choice. That delight is not met when people "chose what I did not delight in" (65:12), and met in those "who choose the things that please me" (56:4). The noun *ḥēpheṣ* names his settled purpose: "he shall fulfill all my purpose" (Isaiah 44:28). It names what a man cares about, and that stops at his death: "what do they care for their houses after them" (Job 21:21).
- **Good, said of the eye.** "Whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor" (Proverbs 22:9). "Bountiful" is literally "good" (10.6).
- **God's delight in a person.** It is the thanks of the rescued: "he rescued me, because he delighted in me" (Psalm 18:19). It is the mockers' taunt over a sufferer: "let him rescue him, for he delights in him!" (Psalm 22:8). The claim is the same. The sufferer does not answer the mockers; he answers God: "Yet you are he who took me from the womb" (22:9) (13.1).
- **An offering.** "For you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it" (Psalm 51:16). Three verses on: "then will you delight in right sacrifices, in burnt offerings and whole burnt offerings" (51:19). It is the same offering. Between the two stands "a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" (51:17) (13.1).
- **Being well pleased.** The Greek *eudokeō* is the Father's word over the Son: "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased" (Matthew 3:17). It is also Paul's word for weaknesses he had pleaded three times to lose: "I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities" (2 Corinthians 12:10). Between his pleading and his contentment stands the answer, "My grace is sufficient for you" (12:9) (10.1).
- **Choosing a person.** God chooses "before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him" (Ephesians 1:4). He chooses people who are "blind, yet have eyes" (Isaiah 43:8, 10), and "those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith" (James 2:5). People choose by what they can already see: "men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom" (Acts 6:3). Section 10.7 sets this out.
- **Holiness.** It is the purpose of being chosen: "that we should be holy and blameless before him" (Ephesians 1:4). It is also a name the chosen already carry, while the inner qualities are still to be put on: "Put on then, as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts" (Colossians 3:12). The verses do not say how the two fit.
- **Desire beside a choice.** The soul's desire for meat is given room away from the place God chose: "you may eat within your towns whenever you desire" (Deuteronomy 12:21). The same words for the soul's desire draw a Levite to that place: "he may come when he desires" (18:6). And the soul's delight goes with a wrong choice: "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations" (Isaiah 66:3). Section 10.7 sets this out.
- **Despising.** Michal "despised him in her heart" when she saw the chosen king dancing before the Lord (2 Samuel 6:16). The same verb describes the servant, "one deeply despised", before whom kings will bow (Isaiah 49:7). People despise the chosen people, judging that God has rejected them (Jeremiah 33:24). And the chosen people themselves "despised the pleasant land" (Psalm 106:24). Each verse gives its own ground: honour before people, a verdict drawn from ruin, no faith in the promise.
- **Knowing that a choice was made.** Peter's hearers know it, and a quarrel ends in silence: "you know that in the early days God made a choice among you" (Acts 15:7, 12). Paul knows it of others from what he saw: "we know … that he has chosen you, because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power" (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5). Cyrus is called for the sake of the chosen "though you do not know me" (Isaiah 45:4). The world hates the chosen "because they do not know him who sent me" (John 15:21).
- **Precious.** The Hebrew *yāqār* is wisdom weighed above *"nothing you desire"* (Proverbs 3:15), the word *"rare in those days"* (1 Samuel 3:1), a visit kept *seldom* (Proverbs 25:17), *"the moon moving in splendor"* that entices a heart (Job 31:26–27), a name *"highly esteemed"* (1 Samuel 18:30), *"the lordly price"* set on a shepherd (Zechariah 11:13), and a son *"dear"* while spoken against (Jeremiah 31:20). The Greek *timios* is faith tested by fire (1 Peter 1:7), the blood of Christ (1:19), and the jewels of Babylon (Revelation 17:4). What differs is who values, what the thing is weighed against, and whether its worth is known: man does not know wisdom's worth (Job 28:13), and Saul would not give the esteem the others gave (1 Samuel 18:29–30). (10.6 *Precious*.)
- **The story around it.** A single verse rarely settles which face a word wears. Jeremiah 18:8–18 does, and so does Genesis 50:20.

Greed harms more than the greedy. It takes the greedy man's own life: "Such are the ways of everyone who is greedy for unjust gain; it takes away the life of its possessors" (Proverbs 1:19). It reaches his house: "Whoever is greedy for unjust gain troubles his own household, but he who hates bribes will live" (Proverbs 15:27). It destroys others: Ezekiel's princes are "like wolves tearing the prey, shedding blood, destroying lives to get dishonest gain" (Ezekiel 22:27). The answer in Proverbs 15:27 is not having no desires. It is a counter-desire: the man who "hates" bribes. Chapter 2 ("Life weighed", "Living before God") gives the account.

section: Pride and the lifted-up heart and spirit
paragraph: The king of Tyre is lamented in the same way. *"You were in Eden, the garden of God; every precious stone was your covering"* (Ezekiel 28:13). *"You were blameless in your ways from the day you were created, till unrighteousness was found in you"* (28:15). *"In the abundance of your trade you were filled with violence in your midst, and you sinned"* (28:16). *"Your heart was proud because of your beauty; you corrupted your wisdom for the sake of your splendor"* (28:17). The covering was prepared for him on the day he was made. The heart took the beauty as its ground, and wisdom was spent for splendour. I read the order the verses give: given, blameless, then trade, violence and a proud heart.

**At its worst.** Ezekiel speaks to the shepherds of Israel: "Ah, shepherds of Israel who have been feeding yourselves! Should not shepherds feed the sheep?" (Ezekiel 34:2). The charge lists the care not given: "The weak you have not strengthened, the sick you have not healed, the injured you have not bound up, the strayed you have not brought back, the lost you have not sought, and with force and harshness you have ruled them" (34:4). The rulers were there, yet "they were scattered, because there was no shepherd" (34:5). I read rule that serves the ruler as counted as no shepherding at all. The proverb sees the same from below: "Like a roaring lion or a charging bear is a wicked ruler over a poor people". The next verse names what lies behind it: "A ruler who lacks understanding is a cruel oppressor, but he who hates unjust gain will prolong his days" (Proverbs 28:15–16). The Preacher watched it with his heart: "when man had power over man to his hurt" (Ecclesiastes 8:9; Chapter 4).

**Its limits, and whose the ruled are.** The law gives the limit three times, each on another ground: the ruler's fear of God (Leviticus 25:43), brotherhood, "over your brothers the people of Israel you shall not rule, one over another ruthlessly" (25:46), and the onlooker, "He shall not rule ruthlessly over him in your sight" (25:53). Behind all three: "For it is to me that the people of Israel are servants" (25:55). A master is told to "stop your threatening, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven" (Ephesians 6:9). Where the limit is gone, the verses name what rose in its place. The shepherds fed themselves, did not strengthen the weak or seek the lost, "and with force and harshness you have ruled them", and the sheep "were scattered, because there was no shepherd" (Ezekiel 34:2–5). "A ruler who lacks understanding is a cruel oppressor, but he who hates unjust gain will prolong his days" (Proverbs 28:16).

**He does what pleases him.**
- *"The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the Lord; he turns it wherever he will"* (Proverbs 21:1). The word for "will" is the word for delight. The next verse: *"Every way of a man is right in his own eyes, but the Lord weighs the heart"* (21:2).
- Job: *"But he is unchangeable, and who can turn him back? What he desires, that he does"* (Job 23:13). Job does not take it as comfort: *"Therefore I am terrified at his presence"* (23:15).
- The sailors, before they throw Jonah into the sea: *"O Lord, let us not perish for this man's life, and lay not on us innocent blood, for you, O Lord, have done as it pleased you"* (Jonah 1:14). Afterwards *"the men feared the Lord exceedingly"* (1:16).
- Balaam: "When Balaam saw that it pleased the Lord to bless Israel, he did not go, as at other times, to look for omens" (Numbers 24:1). What pleased the Lord was to bless, and seeing it turned a man from his omens (10.7).
- Of his servant: *"Yet it was the will of the Lord to crush him; he has put him to grief; when his soul makes an offering for guilt, he shall see his offspring; he shall prolong his days; the will of the Lord shall prosper in his hand"* (Isaiah 53:10). Both times, "the will of the Lord" is the delight word. The verse does not explain it, and I leave it as it stands.
- Of Eli's sons: *"But they would not listen to the voice of their father, for it was the will of the Lord to put them to death"* (1 Samuel 2:25). "Will" is the delight word again. Their father had just said, *"if someone sins against the Lord, who can intercede for him?"*, and the next verse sets Samuel beside them, growing *"in favor with the Lord and also with man"* (2:26). Set beside *"I have no pleasure in the death of anyone"* (Ezekiel 18:32), the two verses seem to pull apart. I do not reconcile them. They stand as Isaiah 53:10 stands.

Many verses speak of the burning anger as turning. Moses asked it: "Turn from your burning anger and relent" (Exodus 32:12). Hezekiah acted for it: "Now it is in my heart to make a covenant with the Lord … in order that his fierce anger may turn away from us" (2 Chronicles 29:10). The king of Nineveh hoped for it with no promise: "Who knows? God may turn and relent and turn from his fierce anger, so that we may not perish" (Jonah 3:9).

Returning comes with no guarantee. Joel says, "Who knows whether he will not turn and relent" (Joel 2:14). The king of Nineveh, with no promise at all, says the same: "Who knows? God may turn and relent and turn from his fierce anger, so that we may not perish" (Jonah 3:9). "When God saw what they did, how they turned from their evil way, God relented" (3:10).

Gathered together, the verses show a person responding to God's anger in these ways. Each is stated by its own verses.
- **Pleading:** "Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak" (Genesis 18:30).
- **Humbling oneself:** "when he humbled himself the wrath of the Lord turned from him" (2 Chronicles 12:12).
- **Acting to remove the cause:** Hezekiah's covenant (2 Chronicles 29:10).
- **Reading the ruin:** "Why has the Lord done thus to this land? What caused the heat of this great anger?" (Deuteronomy 29:24).
- **Crying out from distress:** "when the people of Israel cried out to the Lord, the Lord raised up a deliverer" (Judges 3:9).
- **Refusing the warning,** "until there was no remedy" (2 Chronicles 36:16).
- **Asking for correction without the anger:** "Correct me, O Lord, but in justice; not in your anger" (Jeremiah 10:24).
- **Fearing being cast off:** "Turn not your servant away in anger" (Psalm 27:9).
- **Asking how long:** "How long, O Lord? Will you be angry forever?" (Psalm 79:5).
- **Standing in awe:** "Who can stand before you when once your anger is roused?" (Psalm 76:7).
- **Taking it into the whole of life:** "For all our days pass away under your wrath" (Psalm 90:9), and the prayer, "So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom" (90:12).
- **Sheltering while it passes:** "hide yourselves for a little while until the fury has passed by" (Isaiah 26:20).
- **Holding a false peace:** "surely his anger has turned from me" (Jeremiah 2:35).
- **Mourning:** "For this put on sackcloth, lament and wail" (Jeremiah 4:8).
- **Not taking it in:** "it burned him up, but he did not take it to heart" (Isaiah 42:25).
- **Coming to know:** "And they shall know that I am the Lord" (Ezekiel 5:13).
- **Returning without a guarantee:** "Who knows?" (Jonah 3:9).
- **Bearing it because of one's sin:** "I will bear the indignation of the Lord because I have sinned against him, until he pleads my cause" (Micah 7:9).
- **Leaving vengeance to God:** "never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God" (Romans 12:19), and then, "if your enemy is hungry, feed him" (12:20).
- **Putting off what the wrath comes on:** "But now you must put them all away: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth" (Colossians 3:8), two verses after "On account of these the wrath of God is coming" (3:6).
- **Singing that it is just:** "Just and true are your ways" (Revelation 15:3).
- **Speaking of it as a wrath one is delivered from:** "Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come" (1 Thessalonians 1:10).

What answers these wishes is seldom death.
- **Elijah** is given food, twice: "Arise and eat". He goes "in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights" (1 Kings 19:5–8).
- **Jonah's** wish came with his anger at God's mercy: "angry enough to die" (Jonah 4:9). He is given a question about God's pity for Nineveh (Jonah 4:10–11).
- **Israel**, wishing they had died beside the meat pots of Egypt, is given bread from heaven (Exodus 16:3–4).
- When Israel loathed the manna and spoke against God, the answer was something to look at: "everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live" (Numbers 21:8).

Desire can take hold in the heart before anything is done. Jesus says, "everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart" (Matthew 5:28). The way in is the eye, and he goes straight on: "If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away" (5:29). Proverbs warns a son in the same order, heart and eyes: "Do not desire her beauty in your heart, and do not let her capture you with her eyelashes" (Proverbs 6:25). The Preacher uses the hunter's picture for the other side of that capture: "the woman whose heart is snares and nets, and whose hands are fetters. He who pleases God escapes her, but the sinner is taken by her" (Ecclesiastes 7:26). He names it as his own finding, after he had "turned my heart to know and to search out" (7:25). The escape he names is not strength of will but pleasing God.

Scripture does speak of people alive before God after death, and it uses both words.
- John sees "under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God", crying out for justice (Revelation 6:9–10).
- Hebrews speaks of "the spirits of the righteous made perfect" (Hebrews 12:23).
- Peter speaks of "the spirits in prison" (1 Peter 3:19).
- And Jesus: "do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul" (Matthew 10:28).

paragraph:
Fear of other people takes several forms in the verses.
- **Fear of man.** "who are you that you are afraid of man who dies" (Isaiah 51:12). "do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul" (Matthew 10:28).
- **Fear for another.** Eli trembled for the ark (1 Samuel 4:13). Jeremiah grieved for his people: "For the wound of the daughter of my people is my heart wounded; I mourn, and dismay has taken hold on me" (Jeremiah 8:21). Paul: "I am afraid that as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your thoughts will be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ" (2 Corinthians 11:3).
- **Fear used as a tool.** "he was hired, that I should be afraid and act in this way and sin" (Nehemiah 6:13).
- **Respect owed.** The same word as fear is rendered "respect" toward people. "respect to whom respect is owed, honor to whom honor is owed" (Romans 13:7). "Servants, be subject to your masters with all respect, not only to the good and gentle but also to the unjust" (1 Peter 2:18). Toward parents: "Every one of you shall revere his mother and his father" (Leviticus 19:3).
- **Respect and no fear, two verses apart.** "Have no fear of them, nor be troubled, but in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect" (1 Peter 3:14–15). In Greek, "fear" and "respect" are the same word. The verse does not say whether the respect is toward the one who asks or toward God.
- **Being feared.** Being feared works on the one who is feared. "The horror you inspire has deceived you, and the pride of your heart" (Jeremiah 49:16).

paragraph:
The verses show fear changing character, and they point to what changes it.
- **What it is turned toward.** At the sea Israel "feared greatly" as Egypt marched, and after the crossing "the people feared the Lord, and they believed in the Lord" (Exodus 14:10, 31). In between, fear spoke as a preference: "it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness" (14:12; 10.6, *Shaped by fear*). In the boat, fear of the storm became fear of the one who stilled it (Mark 4:41). In these cases the change came after God acted.
- **One fear set in place of another, by the same speaker.** "Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you" (Exodus 20:20). "do not fear what they fear … Let him be your fear" (Isaiah 8:12–13). "Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell", and then, "Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows" (Matthew 10:28, 31).
- **Who speaks to it, and why.** God's "for I am with you" (Isaiah 41:10), and Jael's "do not be afraid" (Judges 4:18).
- **Who meets it.** "When justice is done, it is a joy to the righteous but terror to evildoers" (Proverbs 21:15). One scroll was read aloud: the officials "turned one to another in fear", and "neither the king nor any of his servants who heard all these words was afraid" (Jeremiah 36:16, 24). At the signs of the end, "people fainting with fear", and to the disciples, "straighten up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near" (Luke 21:26, 28).
- **One's own conduct.** "rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad" (Romans 13:3). "I also will choose harsh treatment for them and bring their fears upon them, because when I called, no one answered" (Isaiah 66:4). The same passage opens with the one God looks to, who "trembles at my word" (66:2). I read the passage as setting that trembling beside "their fears".
- **Pride.** "So do not become proud, but fear" (Romans 11:20). "The horror you inspire has deceived you, and the pride of your heart" (Jeremiah 49:16).
- **Where the heart is.** Fear "taught by men" while "their hearts are far from me", against fear put "in their hearts" (Isaiah 29:13; Jeremiah 32:40).
- **Faith, trust and love** (the section above).
- **Joy or silence.** The women left the tomb "with fear and great joy, and ran to tell his disciples" (Matthew 28:8). In Mark's account "they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid" (Mark 16:8). The two accounts stand side by side.
- **The same root, rendered as another movement.** *Rāgaz*, "to tremble", is also anger and grief (Psalm 4:4; 2 Samuel 18:33). *Paḥad*, "dread", is also "thrill" (Isaiah 60:5). *Phobos*, "fear", is also "respect" (Romans 13:7).

paragraph: **He chooses his servant with delight, and puts his Spirit on him.** Matthew applies Isaiah's words to Jesus: "Behold, my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved with whom my soul is well pleased. I will put my Spirit upon him, and he will proclaim justice to the Gentiles" (Matthew 12:18, quoting Isaiah 42:1). The one verse holds the one who chooses, whose soul is well pleased; the servant he has chosen, whom Matthew sees fulfilled in Jesus; and his Spirit, put upon him. Matthew gives the setting. The Pharisees "conspired against him, how to destroy him" (Matthew 12:14). Jesus, "aware of this, withdrew", healed them all, and "ordered them not to make him known" (12:15–16). "This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah" (12:17), and the words go on: "He will not quarrel or cry aloud … a bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench, until he brings justice to victory" (12:19–20).

section: Loving and hating one's own soul
paragraph: One more thread surprised me. In Proverbs, loving your own soul is wisdom: "Whoever gets sense loves his own soul" (Proverbs 19:8). "He who fails to find me injures himself" (Proverbs 8:36). In the Gospels the same words seem to reverse: "Whoever loves his life loses it, and whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life" (John 12:25). The other Gospels put it as wanting: "whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will find it" (Matthew 16:25; Mark 8:35; Luke 9:24). Paul lives it: "I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course" (Acts 20:24).

**A will redirected.** Jesus takes the will to be first and the will to follow, and turns them.
- The disciples "had argued with one another about who was the greatest". "If anyone would be first, he must be last of all and servant of all" (Mark 9:34–35). "whoever would be first among you must be slave of all. For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve" (Mark 10:44–45; Matthew 20:27–28).
- After Peter was told "you are not setting your mind on the things of God": "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me. For whoever would save his life will lose it" (Matthew 16:23–25; Mark 8:34–35; Luke 9:23–24, "daily").
The will is not removed. Its aim is named, wanting to be first, wanting to save one's life, and it is given another way to that end.

**The Father's will, said of creation and of people.** "for you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created" (Revelation 4:11). "God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose" (1 Corinthians 12:18). "God chose to make known how great among the Gentiles are the riches of the glory of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory" (Colossians 1:27). Christ "gave himself for our sins … according to the will of our God and Father" (Galatians 1:4). God "desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth" (1 Timothy 2:4). And after the shepherd who rejoices over the one found: "So it is not the will of my Father who is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish" (Matthew 18:14).

The same feeling is not always the same thing.
- **Anger** can heal, as Jesus's does (Mark 3:5). It can stop its ears and stone a man (Acts 7:57–58). It can be "a rage that has reached up to heaven" (2 Chronicles 28:9). "Be angry and do not sin" (Ephesians 4:26) tells me anger itself is not forbidden. What it does, and how long it stays, is the question.
- **Indignation** is the disciples' complaint at a woman's gift: "Why this waste?" (Matthew 26:8). It is also one of the fruits of a grief that turns to God: "what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal" (2 Corinthians 7:11).
- **Vexation**, *ka'as*, is what a person does to another ("her rival used to provoke her grievously", 1 Samuel 1:6), what a person bears ("I have been speaking out of my great anxiety and vexation", 1:16), and even something that does good: "Sorrow is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad" (Ecclesiastes 7:3). The verse before gives the house of mourning its reason: "for this is the end of all mankind, and the living will lay it to heart" (7:2).
- **Fear** is forbidden and commanded, sometimes in one sentence (Exodus 20:20). The word for the fear that makes people run is the word for the fear that keeps them from turning away. The section on fear above sets out what changes it.
- **Anxiety** is rebuked when it is for my own food and clothing (Matthew 6:25), and praised when it is for the welfare of others (Philippians 2:20). It is the same Greek word. The Hebrew word for anxious dread is also the word for being sorry for sin (Psalm 38:18). The section on anxiety above sets out the difference.
- **Provoking** is what love does not do. It "is not irritable" (1 Corinthians 13:5). Yet believers are told, "let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works" (Hebrews 10:24), with the same Greek word.
- **Delight** is set on God's commandments by the man who fears him (Psalm 112:1), and on war by the peoples God scatters (Psalm 68:30). The same claim about God's delight is thanks in one psalm and a taunt in another (Psalm 18:19; 22:8). The section on delight above sets out what it is set on.
The word used for Jesus' indignation is used for the disciples at the woman's ointment (Matthew 26:8) and for the ruler of the synagogue at a healing (Luke 13:14). One word is aimed three ways.

In the Gospels Jesus' anger is described in human words. Twice the verses name it.
- **At hardness of heart, with grief.** Asked whether it was lawful on the Sabbath "to save life or to kill", they were silent. "And he looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart, and said to the man, 'Stretch out your hand'" (Mark 3:4–5). The anger and the grief have the same object, and the act that follows is a healing. The next verse is the plot: "The Pharisees went out and immediately held counsel with the Herodians against him, how to destroy him" (3:6).
- **For the children.** "When Jesus saw it, he was indignant and said to them, 'Let the children come to me; do not hinder them'" (Mark 10:14).

And it happens before Jesus' acts. In the boat the disciples were first afraid of the storm: "Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?" (Mark 4:38). Then he stilled it, and "they were filled with great fear and said to one another, 'Who then is this?'" (4:41). The same people, with the same word, are afraid twice, and the second fear is of him.
